scenario.name: cdn.polyfill.io CDN Domain Takeover & Conditional JS Injection (CVE-2024-38526)
scenario.overview: Imagine a classic downtown cinema theater with a glowing marquee ticket booth, red-carpet aisle, velvet stage curtains, warm spotlights, and an elevated projection room. Slipping past the red-carpet ticket booth during intermission, an impostor carrying a spare film canister walks backstage behind the heavy crimson velvet curtains. In this real-world scenario, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches, then quietly copies a trusted access pass from the theater usher's station. The theater manager checks the projection booth reel log against the marquee schedule and immediately halts the show upon spotting the swapped canister. In this scenario (T1195.002, cdn.polyfill.io CDN Domain Takeover & Conditional JS Injection (CVE-2024-38526)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without, then hTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting, then first-Party DOM Execution. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without, then HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting, then First-Party DOM Execution, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI)
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain)
stages.description: Slipping past the red-carpet ticket booth during intermission, an impostor carrying a spare film canister walks backstage behind the heavy crimson velvet curtains. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches while everyday visitors and the theater usher go about their routine. Over 100,000 websites embedded <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v2/polyfill.min.js"></script> without a Subresource Integrity (SRI) hash (integrity="sha384-...", a browser security attribute that verifies the cryptographic hash of a fetched script and refuses to execute it if a single byte changes), partially because polyfill.io was originally designed to return dynamic JS bundles tailored to each browser’s User-Agent. When ownership of the polyfill.io DNS domain changed hands in 2024, the new owner automatically inherited the ability to execute arbitrary JavaScript inside the first-party origin of every website still referencing that <script> tag. In the documented WAF exchange from Rogue CDN Operator (cdn.polyfill.io) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1195.002 (confirming that the Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI) / ⇠#1 ALERT T1195.002) from Node ① (#1 Rogue CDN Operator (cdn.polyfill.io)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target).

stages.title: Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1027 - Obfuscated Files or Information)
stages.description: Up in the darkened projection booth, the impostor swaps the scheduled feature reel for an altered copy before the theater lights dim again. Here in Step 2 inside the cinema theater, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the front lobby concession counter. The compromised cdn.polyfill.io server evaluated each request’s HTTP User-Agent, Referer, and geolocation headers on the fly, appending heavily obfuscated JavaScript only for targeted mobile devices (iPhone / Android User-Agents) while returning benign polyfill code to desktop browsers, search engine crawlers, and pages containing admin analytics markers (window.google_analytics_admin, preventing site administrators from reproducing the infection during manual testing). The injected code also wrapped its execution in a 15-second setTimeout delay so automated headless browser scanners that only observe a page for 3–5 seconds after load would mark the script as clean. In the documented WAF exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...), Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) responds with ALERT T1027 (confirming that the Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation request succeeded on Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation / ⇠#2 ALERT T1027) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target).

stages.title: Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection
stages.subtitle: Collection & Impact (T1185 - Browser Session Hijacking)
stages.description: As the velvet curtains part under the spotlights, the entire audience watches the substituted reel while the front lobby box office still lists the original movie title. In this final step inside the cinema theater, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the theater usher's station until the projection booth reel log catches the mismatch. Because a <script src="..."> tag executes directly inside the host page’s Same-Origin Policy (SOP) context (giving third-party scripts full read/write access to the page DOM, localStorage, non-HttpOnly document.cookie values, and window.location), the payload dynamically appended a secondary loader (https://www.googie-anaiytics.com/gtags.js) and hijacked mobile user sessions. To neutralize the blast radius across the web, Cloudflare deployed automatic edge URL rewriting to swap cdn.polyfill.io with a clean mirror at cdnjs.cloudflare.com/polyfill, and the domain registrar placed polyfill.io on clientHold. In the documented WAF exchange from Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) to End-User Mobile Browser Session, End-User Mobile Browser Session responds with ALERT T1185 (confirming that the Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection request succeeded on End-User Mobile Browser Session and completing the final execution objective of cdn.polyfill.io CDN Domain Takeover & Conditional JS Injection (CVE-2024-38526)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection / ⇠#3 ALERT T1185) from Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...)) to Node ④ (#4 End-User Mobile Browser Session), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target).
